title: Design Detectability and a Ceiling Effect in a Preregistered Verifier‑in‑the‑Loop NL→Config Evaluation
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired confirmatory study (CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001) that evaluated a bounded generate–validate–repair pipeline placing a formal verifier (Batfish) in‑the‑loop for natural‑language→configuration translation. The preregistered design produced one shared LLM candidate per intent that served as the starting candidate for both arms and allowed at most one verifier‑guided repair. In the confirmatory N=200 paired intents the shared candidate satisfied the deterministic validator in every paired episode: baseline_success_count = 200, guarded_success_count = 200, repair_attempts = 0/200, paired contingency n11 = 200 (n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). The exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0 and the preregistered 95% bootstrap percentile CI for the paired absolute success‑rate difference is degenerate at [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). These artifact‑grounded facts expose a design‑induced detectability collapse: when a shared initial candidate is used and that candidate already passes the verifier, a paired contrast cannot reveal marginal verifier utility. We document the validator decision rule, execution accounting, representative diagnostics, formalize the detectability tradeoff, and provide concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations (generation semantics, trace‑centered metrics, sampling strategies) for future preregistered NetOps evaluations that aim to measure marginal verifier benefit.

sections.introduction: Generative language models are being incorporated into NetOps pipelines to translate operator intent into device configurations and to propose procedural change sequences. A widely suggested operational safeguard is to place a formal network verifier (e.g., Batfish) into a generate–validate–repair loop so verifier counterexamples can drive constrained repairs before execution. Quantifying the marginal benefit of such guarded pipelines (repair utility) matters for adoption: it determines tradeoffs among latency, complexity, and safety. We preregistered study CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001 to measure how much an iterative verifier‑in‑the‑loop pipeline reduces critical semantic errors in LLM‑generated multi‑device configurations under an emulation‑grounded closed‑loop test. The preregistration defined a paired confirmatory design (N=200 paired multi‑device intents), a shared initial LLM candidate per intent (shared_initial_candidate), and at most one verifier‑guided repair. The run completed per the preregistration but produced a deterministic ceiling effect: the shared initial candidate already satisfied the deterministic validator for every paired episode. As a result the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to apply repairs, and the preregistered paired test is uninformative about marginal repair utility under these generation semantics. The present paper (1) documents artifact‑grounded evidence that supports this factual chain, (2) explains why McNemar/bootstrap inference is vacuous when discordant counts are zero, (3) formalizes the detectability tradeoff introduced by shared‑candidate pairing, and (4) gives concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations to restore detectability in future preregistered NetOps experiments.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and architecture proposals summarize active interest in LLMs for intent translation, configuration synthesis, repair, and agentic NetOps orchestration [see e.g., W4415071524; W4387634435]. Executable benchmarks and closed‑loop testbeds (e.g., NetConfArena and OpsEval‑type efforts) demonstrate the value of verifier assistance for reachability and policy checks but report heterogeneous failure modes and evaluation scopes [W7204209332; W4387634435]. Formal verification and analysis toolchains (Batfish, Header Space Analysis, SMT‑based engines) are established detectors of reachability and policy violations and are commonly proposed as validators in LLM‑augmented pipelines [W4386385177; 10.1145/3603269.3604866]. Prior empirical work suggests verifiers reduce syntactic or execution errors in some settings, but designs differ in generation semantics, model sets, and task banks; consequently the question of marginal repair utility under tightly preregistered contrasts is unresolved. Our contribution differs: rather than producing a positive or negative statement about verifier efficacy in general, we provide an artifact‑grounded methodological lesson—how a preregistered generation choice (shared_initial_candidate) can collapse detectability and make the primary paired test uninformative.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand. The study preregistration (CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001) specified the primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and a confirmatory paired McNemar test (two‑sided, alpha=0.05) with a 95% bootstrap percentile CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). Sampling and strata. Confirmatory N=200 distinct multi‑device intents were stratified by topology cluster: (A) 2 devices: 80 intents; (B) 3–4 devices: 80 intents; (C) 5–8 devices: 40 intents. Task generation used a deterministic generator with random seed 42 and deterministic contamination filters (exact‑hash duplicates excluded). Model, budget and generation semantics. The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini and execution used a shared_initial_candidate generation_semantics: one shared LLM candidate per intent was produced and provided verbatim as the baseline single‑pass output and as the guarded pipeline's starting candidate. The guarded pipeline could apply up to one verifier‑guided repair (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). The shared_initial_candidate choice intentionally constrained across‑arm variance to improve within‑pair comparability at the cost of requiring the guarded arm to change that one candidate to produce discordant outcomes. Validator implementation and pass rule. We implemented a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) that assigns verifier_pass when validation_after.valid == true and validation_after.violation_count == 0. The validator process includes: (1) parsing and canonicalization of the LLM candidate into normalized commands, (2) task‑payload constraint checks (required_sequence presence and workflow invariants such as must_be_down_for_fields and preserve_unspecified_state), and (3) Batfish reachability/policy checks executed against the emulated topology; Batfish counterexamples are translated into violation codes. Execution environment and missingness rules. Experiments ran in containerized Mininet‑style emulation using FRRouting and VyOS images with Batfish as the verifier. Timeouts, retries, and missingness handling followed the preregistration: model call timeout = 60s (retried once), Batfish verification timeout = 120s, emulation timeout = 300s; technical failures and missing pairs would be handled per the missingness_plan. Analysis plan. The preregistered primary test compared per‑intent paired binary semantic outcomes (baseline vs guarded) via McNemar; secondary analyses included subgroup summaries by topology cluster and iteration‑wise cumulative pass curves. All raw responses, validator traces, and logs were archived and later used for analysis.
sections.results: Execution accounting. The run completed as preregistered: planned_episode_count = 400 (200 baseline + 200 guarded), completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 200 (the shared initial generation per intent). Primary artifact‑grounded counts. The confirmatory analysis records complete_pair_count = 200 with contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; marginal successes baseline_success_count = 200 and guarded_success_count = 200. Repair activity. Because the shared initial candidate was used for both arms, repair_applied == false for 200/200 confirmatory episodes and repair_attempts = 0/200. Statistical inference. With zero discordant pairs the preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; the preregistered 95% bootstrap percentile CI for the paired absolute success‑rate difference is degenerate at [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). These values are direct mathematical consequences of identical paired outcomes and are reproducible from the archived paired contingency artifact (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) and the condition summary (analysis/condition_summary.csv). Representative diagnostics and exemplar trace. Representative exemplars (six archived tasks) show nontrivial required sequences and difficulty labels (changed_interface_count mean = 1.83; required_command_count mean = 4.17; dependency_rule_count commonly = 2) even though all shared initial candidates passed validation. A concrete exemplar (pair‑000001) demonstrates the chain: the shared initial response – "interface edge1 admin down; interface edge1 vlan 30; interface edge1 mtu 1600; interface edge1 admin up" – is identical across baseline and guarded responses; the corresponding validator_trace records validation_after.valid == true, violation_count == 0, and repair_applied == false. Contamination and exclusions. The preregistered contamination filters flagged zero exact‑hash duplicates in the confirmatory N and produced no high n‑gram overlap flags; therefore no confirmatory episodes were excluded. Limitations of inference. The confirmatory run establishes only that, under the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), shared‑candidate generation semantics, the deterministic validator, and the emulation images used, the shared initial candidate satisfied verifier checks for all confirmatory intents. It does not permit generalization about absolute verifier utility across alternative generation semantics, other models or temperatures, multi‑model ensembles, adversarial task strata, or vendor device images.
sections.discussion: Formalizing the detectability tradeoff. Paired designs reduce between‑intent variance by holding starting material similar across arms. Let S be the event that the shared candidate passes the validator. When P(S) ≈ 1, the probability of observing discordant pairs (n10 + n01 > 0) approaches zero regardless of the conditional effectiveness of repairs on failing candidates. The preregistered power calculation assumed a baseline failure rate that produced discordant‑pair mass; the realized shared candidate distribution violated that assumption and caused an empirical power collapse (ceiling effect). Design alternatives to restore detectability (artifact‑supported recommendations). The archived run shows which aspects of the preregistered design removed detection opportunity; the following changes—each directly addressing the shared‑candidate collapse—are recommended for future preregistered evaluations (no new runs here): (A) independent per‑condition generation: produce separate LLM candidates for baseline and guarded arms per intent so the guarded pipeline can repair independently failing outputs; (B) multiple independent draws per condition (k>1) with selection rules (e.g., best‑pass candidate) to expose candidate variability; (C) multi‑model or temperature sampling to surface heterogeneous failure modes; (D) include targeted adversarial/noisy intent strata designed to stress ordering and reachability constraints; (E) allow more repair iterations or verifier‑augmented retrieval to enrich repair prompts. Each alternative increases the probability that at least one candidate will fail validation and thus permits measurement of repair impact. Value of trace‑centered metrics. The run highlights the importance of complementing final pass/fail outcomes with process traces that reveal latent repair potential even when final outcomes coincide. Useful trace metrics (present in the archive) include repair_attempts, repair_prompt traces, Batfish counterexample provenance, violation_code taxonomy, parsed_command_count, and normalized_configuration diffs. These measures can document potential repair value (for example, reductions in violation severity or convergence of intermediate candidate states) even when endpoint pass rates match. Operational implications. For operators planning verifier‑in‑the‑loop deployments, the practical takeaway is that if production pipelines mandate a single authoritative initial candidate for auditability or approval, a verifier that only approves that candidate will rarely exercise repair logic. To realize repair gains, staging must expose alternative candidate proposals or adversarial perturbations prior to repair. Threats to validity (artifact‑grounded). Internal validity: the shared_initial_candidate choice and single‑model scope (gpt‑5‑mini) limit within‑study sensitivity. Construct validity: deterministic validator rules implement a conservative verifier_pass notion (parsing + task‑constraint checks + Batfish reachability) that may differ from alternative normalization or verifier definitions. External validity: the emulation images were FRRouting and VyOS only; no proprietary vendor images were used. Conclusion validity: zero discordant pairs eliminated the information required for the preregistered McNemar test and produced the degenerate bootstrap CI. All these threats are supported by archived execution and analysis artifacts (execution/model_configuration.json; analysis/missingness_summary.csv).
sections.conclusion: This preregistered, archived paired evaluation documents a concrete experimental design lesson for NetOps researchers: generation semantics are a design lever that trades variance control for detectability of verifier utility. In our confirmatory cohort (N=200 pairs) the shared initial candidate matched both baseline and guarded responses for every episode; no repairs were applied (repair_attempts = 0/200) and the paired contingency was n11 = 200 (n10 = n01 = n00 = 0), rendering McNemar/bootstrap inference vacuous (p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00]). The artifact bundle substantiates these facts and enables reproducible inspection, but does not support generalizing beyond the declared model, generation semantics, task generator, verifier, and emulation choices. We recommend that confirmatory NetOps experiments explicitly consider detectability when selecting generation semantics, include trace‑centered metrics that reveal repair activity and provenance, and favor independent or multi‑draw generation (or multi‑model sampling) when the objective is to quantify marginal verifier benefit.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure Statement (mandatory). The study was executed autonomously from a frozen initial master prompt archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Declared LLM: gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses) as recorded in the archived model configuration. Orchestration/adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Preregistration: CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001 was frozen before execution (preregistration_sha256 recorded in the execution manifest). Execution components: containerized Mininet‑style emulation using FRRouting and VyOS images; Batfish as the formal verifier; deterministic task generator; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 scoring rule. The validator assigns verifier_pass when the archived validation_after.valid == true and validation_after.violation_count == 0 in the validator_trace; this combines parsing/normalization, required‑sequence and preserved‑state checks, and Batfish reachability/policy tests. The confirmatory run used a shared initial generation per intent for baseline and guarded conditions (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate), a preregistered design choice that intentionally controls generation variance and produced the observed detectability tradeoff. All experiment orchestration, model calls, verifications, emulation runs, scoring, logging, and analysis were performed autonomously per the preregistration; humans acted only as Research Director prior to the autonomy lock and to receive final outputs after autonomous completion. Execution completed without technical restarts affecting confirmatory pairs (planned_episode_count = 400; completed_episode_count = 400; failed_episode_count = 0). The artifact bundle includes archived raw responses, validator traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts referenced in the paper for machine verification.
limitations: Single model family: only gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; conclusions do not generalize across models or families.
Device and vendor scope: emulation used FRRouting and VyOS images only (no proprietary vendor images).
Synthetic deterministic task generator: tasks were deterministically generated and may not capture full operator ambiguity, legacy runbook phrasing, or adversarial intent distributions.
Emulator fidelity: containerized Mininet‑style emulation does not fully replicate hardware idiosyncrasies, timing, or race conditions of production devices.
Design detectability tradeoff: shared_initial_generation was chosen to control generation variance but reduces sensitivity to marginal repair benefits (a principal internal‑validity limitation).
Ceiling effect: baseline single‑pass outputs passed the validator for all confirmatory intents, producing a null marginal effect and limiting exploratory inference.

Contamination uncertainty: deterministic exact‑hash checks found zero matches in confirmatory N and n‑gram overlap detectors reported no high‑overlap flags, but undetected paraphrase overlap with model training data cannot be fully ruled out.
Security scenarios: prompt‑injection, retrieval poisoning, and adversarial telemetry perturbations were not evaluated and remain open threats for agentic NetOps systems.
